variables-with-const-and-let-const.title: Use const for bindings that stay put
variables-with-const-and-let-const.bodyMarkdown:
A **variable binding** connects a useful name to a value. Good names make later code easier to read because the code explains what the value means.

```js
const eventName = "Career Fair";
const capacity = 80;

console.log(eventName, capacity);
```

Line by line:

1. `const eventName = "Career Fair";` creates a binding named `eventName` and stores the event title.
2. `const capacity = 80;` stores the event capacity under a second clear name.
3. `console.log(eventName, capacity);` reads both bindings and shows their current values in the Console.

Use `const` when your code does not need to assign a different value to that binding later. This is a good default because it makes accidental reassignment harder.

variables-with-const-and-let-let.title: Use let when the binding must be reassigned
variables-with-const-and-let-let.bodyMarkdown:
Some values are meant to change while a program runs. Imagine tracking how many seats remain after one person registers:

```js
let seatsRemaining = 24;
seatsRemaining = seatsRemaining - 1;
console.log(seatsRemaining);
```

Line by line:

1. `let seatsRemaining = 24;` creates a binding that is allowed to receive a new value later.
2. `seatsRemaining = seatsRemaining - 1;` reads the current value `24`, subtracts `1`, and stores the new value `23` back in the same binding.
3. `console.log(seatsRemaining);` shows the updated value so you can confirm the reassignment happened.

Reassignment is different from declaration: you write `let` only when creating the binding. When you update it later, use the existing name by itself.
